cues.text: Katy, hi. Thanks for inviting me round.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: Thanks for coming know you're up to your neck in finals revision, but I've got to make up my mind about next year's Geography field trip and I'd really like your advice.
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: We've got to choose between an African trip and one in Europe. They've told us a bit about both trips in the lecture but I really can't make up my mind, and I know you did the African one last year.
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: That's right.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: So, where exactly did you go? I mean. I know it was in Kenya, in East Africa ...
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Yes, well, we were right up in the north-west of the country. It was beautiful. We stayed in a place called the Marich Pass Field Studies Centre.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: Right. Dr Rowe said the accommodation was traditional African-style cottages. er. he had a special name for them ..
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Bandas. Yes, they're fine. You have to share two or three people together. They're pretty basic but you have a mosquito net.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: They don't provide spray though so remember to take plenty with you - you'll need it. And there's no electricity in the Field Centre - you’ll have hurricane lamps instead They give a good light, it's no problem.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: What about places to study? Dr Rowe said there was a library ...
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Yes. but it’s quite small. There's a lecture room as well - but most of us worked out in the open air, there are plenty of places outside. And it's so beautiful - you're right in the middle of the forest clearing
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: I gather it's a relatively unmodernised area?
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Definitely. They actually set up the centre there because it's on the boundaries of two distinct ecological zones the mountains, where the people are mainly agriculturalists, and the semi-arid plains lower down, where they're semi nomadic pastoralists.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: So, how much chance did you get to meet the local people there? Did you get die chance to do interviews?
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Yes though we had to use local interpreters. But that was OK. Then we did field observation, of course, looking at environmental and cultural conditions, and morphological mapping.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: What's that?
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Oh. Looking at the surface forms of the landscape, the slope elements and so on.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: What about specific projects?
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Yes. After the first two or three days, we spent most of our time on those. We could pretty well do what we wanted, although they all had to relate to issues concerned with development in some way.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: People did various things .. some were based on social and cultural topics, like the effect of education on the aspirations of young people, and some did more physical process-based studies, looking at things like soil erosion. My group actually looked at issues relating to water, things like sources such as rivers and wells, and quality and so on.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: It was a good project to work on, but, a bit frustrating - we felt we needed a lot more time really.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: Right. Dr Rowe did say something about limiting project scope.
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Yes, he told us that too at the beginning and I can see why now. What else ... well, we had some good trips out as part of the course.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: We went to a market town a place called Sigor - that was to study distribution and to look at agricultural production we went to the Wei Wei valley, that's an important agricultural region.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: And what about animals? Did you have a chance to go to a national park?
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Sure, we did a top on the last day, on the way back to the airport at Nairobi. But actually there was lots of wildlife at the Field Centre vervet monkeys and baboons and lizards ..
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: Mmm. It does sound good.
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: It was excellent, I‘d say. In terms of logistics it was very well run, but it was more than that I mean, it's not the sort of place I‘d ever have got to on my own, and it was a real eye-opener - it got me really interested in development issues and the way other people live.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: I did find it frustrating at the time that we couldn't get as far as we wanted on the project, but actually I'm going to follow it up in my dissertation, so it's given me some ideas and data for that as well.
cues.speaker: Jack

cues.text: So you'd say it was worth the extra money?
cues.speaker: Katy

cues.text: Definitely.
cues.speaker: Jack
